The world is proving that clean energy can scale at record speed. For me, the real test now is whether it can reach the countries and communities still being left behind.
 
I was pleased to participate today in the HLPF 2026 Special Event: “Implementing the Global Plan of Action for the Decade of Sustainable Energy for All to 2030,” which also marked the launch of the UN-Energy Work Programme 2026–2030.
 
The launch comes at a decisive moment for SDG 7. Clean energy is scaling faster than ever: in 2025, the world added 692 GW of new renewable electricity capacity, the largest annual increase on record, with renewables accounting for almost 97% of all new power capacity installed globally.
 
Yet progress remains too uneven. Around 655 million people still lack electricity, nearly 2 billion still rely on polluting cooking fuels, and installed renewable capacity stands at 544 watts per person globally, compared with just 33.6 watts in low-income countries.
 
This is the challenge of the final stretch to 2030.
 
The Global Plan of Action provides the roadmap. The UN-Energy Work Programme provides the coordination platform to help turn that roadmap into delivery through foresight, acceleration, partnerships, data, convening and communications.
 
What stood out to me is how deeply connected these issues have become: energy access, clean cooking, AI and digitalisation, critical minerals, green jobs, finance, gender equality and industrial development. Fragmented action will not deliver the speed or scale required.
 
SDG 7 must also move beyond access to become an engine of opportunity. The global energy sector now employs 76 million people, including at least 16.6 million in renewable energy, but many of these opportunities remain concentrated in economies with established clean-energy value chains.
 
Finance must also reach those furthest behind. International public finance for clean energy in developing countries reached US$24.6 billion in 2024, yet LDCs, LLDCs and SIDS received less than 30% of these flows.
 
At UNDP, we see this through our work supporting 398 energy projects in 131 countries: helping countries turn policy into investment, and investment into development outcomes.
 
The years to 2030 must be about delivery with speed, scale and equity.
